video_title: Knock-On Effects Could Make This Worse Than The Dot-Com Bust | David Rosenberg
gist: David Rosenberg argues US growth is decelerating toward a 1.5% trailing trend with roughly half of remaining growth coming from AI data-center construction and half from an equity wealth effect, while nearly every S&P 500 sector except healthcare and staples has become correlated to the single AI trade — making an unwind potentially broader than the 2000 tech bust. He blames most of the recent 10-year yield backup on a hawkish new Fed chair rather than deficits, expects a bond rally around the November 4 Treasury refunding, and is positioned in Europe, Japan, India, Brazil, healthcare and commodities with zero AI stocks; New Harbor adds that they just bought cheap S&P 7200-strike puts and see gold/silver miners forming cup-and-handle bases.

themes.theme: Growth Turndown Under the AI Veneer

insights.claim: US real GDP is decelerating from a 3% economy toward a four-quarter trailing trend of roughly 1.5% once third-quarter data lands — not a recession, but historically the level at which trading desks start asking what comes next.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A 1-handle growth print would undercut the 'resilient economy' narrative used to justify cyclical exposure and would revive recession-hedging trades.
insights.quote: once we get the third quarter numbers we're going to have a four quarter trailing trend in real GDP of 1 and a.5%

insights.claim: Roughly half of remaining US economic growth comes from AI data-center construction and the other half from the equity wealth effect on high-end consumer spending, leaving the economy dependent on two props rather than broad-based demand.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Both props are the same trade: an equity drawdown or a capex pause hits GDP and markets simultaneously, so equity risk and macro risk are no longer diversifying.

insights.claim: Real consumer spending is growing a bit above 2% only because households are spending against 401k wealth rather than income; matched to disposable income growth, consumer spending growth would be roughly zero, and the personal savings rate has fallen precipitously in the past year.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Consumer-facing earnings are levered to the stock market, not to wages — a market correction transmits to retail and discretionary revenue with almost no lag.
insights.quote: there'd be no growth in consumer spending in the past year

insights.claim: Non-tech business investment is flat year-over-year while real tech spending is up 16%, meaning the AI boom is sapping vitality from the rest of the corporate sector rather than lifting it.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Aggregate capex strength is a composition illusion; non-AI industrial and equipment suppliers should be underwritten as flat-to-declining, not cyclically recovering.
insights.quote: The rest of the corporate spending is flat year-over-year.

insights.claim: The recession that was supposed to follow Fed tightening and yield-curve inversion never arrived because of a roughly $2 trillion COVID stimulus-check shock, and that offset is now in the rearview mirror — the business cycle was postponed, not repealed.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Investors who concluded from 2022-23 that recession signals no longer work are re-running the same trade without the fiscal cushion that saved them.
insights.quote: that was the Energizer Bunny that kept on giving um and that's that's in the rearview mirror right now

insights.claim: The Fed's Beige Book housing commentary is poor and the AI-borrowing-driven rise in mortgage rates hits a housing sector that has powerful economic multipliers despite its small direct GDP share — a leading indicator almost nobody is discussing.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Housing-linked names and rate-sensitive credit are the second-order casualty of AI debt issuance; watch Beige Book and housing data as an early tell on the growth downturn.
insights.quote: How is any of this good for the housing sector

themes.theme: AI Capex Math and Earnings Quality

insights.claim: Backing out the hundreds of billions turning into trillions of AI capital investment implies revenues must balloon roughly 50% a year for the next half decade to generate a decent return — a hurdle Rosenberg considers extremely difficult to clear.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Gives a testable benchmark: track AI-attributable revenue growth against 50% CAGR, and treat shortfalls as the trigger for multiple and estimate compression.
insights.quote: revenues are going to have to balloon uh 50% a year for the next half decade

insights.claim: AI-complex earnings quality is flattered by cross-ownership, circular financing and mark-to-market stock gains booked from one company to the next, although even stripping that out leaves double-digit earnings growth.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Analyst recognition of non-cash and circular revenue is a plausible catalyst for estimate cuts even without a demand slowdown.
insights.quote: there's so much cross ownership and uh circular financing

insights.claim: Caterpillar is the best non-tech leading indicator for the data-center construction boom because it sells so much equipment into it, and its stock is down more than 25% over the past few months.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A free, real-time proxy for AI buildout momentum that is already flashing negative while AI equities remain near highs.
insights.quote: Caterpillar's become a surrogate uh and I would say a leading indicator and its stock is down more than 25%

insights.claim: The Magnificent 7 have done almost nothing over the past six months and, while credit spreads stay tight, credit default swaps on many of these firms have been rising — most notably on Oracle, the poster child for AI leverage.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: CDS widening ahead of cash spreads is the classic early warning; watch AI-issuer CDS as the leading credit signal on the trade.
insights.quote: while credit spreads have remained tight, the dichotomy is that credit default swaps have been rising uh for many of these firms

insights.claim: AI investment has outgrown corporate cash flow and is now funded in the debt markets in long-dated maturities and multiple currencies, turning an enthusiasm bubble into an investment-and-leverage bubble that competes with the government for funds.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Debt-funded capex creates a self-defeating loop — issuance pushes real rates up, which compresses the very multiples supporting the equity story.
insights.quote: it's because it's being financed in the debt markets. That's something that's relatively new compared to where we were four or five months ago.

insights.claim: Rosenberg's base case is a 2027 in which AI earnings estimates come down at the same time the market multiple compresses, a double hit rather than either alone.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Frames the downside as multiplicative — a 20% estimate cut on a rerated multiple is a far larger drawdown than consensus scenario analysis assumes.
insights.quote: I think there's a very good chance that's going to happen. and I would have no problem uh formulating that uh as as a base case.

insights.claim: In the current AI boom only healthcare and consumer staples are uncorrelated with the trade — industrials, financials, consumer discretionary and utilities are all highly correlated — versus the late 1990s when only media and telecom moved with technology, so an unwind would be broader than the early-2000s bust.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Standard sector rotation offers almost no protection this cycle; only healthcare, staples and non-US/hard assets function as genuine diversifiers.
insights.quote: everything outside of healthcare and consumer staples, all these other sectors are correlated with that one trade. Um so where are you going to hide?

insights.claim: The market 'broadening out' that technical strategists celebrated is actually every sector converging onto a single generative-AI trade, and breadth indicators have since started to fade.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Reframes a widely cited bullish signal as a hidden concentration risk — breadth gains here raise, not lower, portfolio correlation.
insights.quote: it's really everything is converging on one trade which is generative AI

insights.claim: Household financial asset mixes are 73% equities versus only 7% bonds per the Fed flow of funds, an all-time stretch that also holds for older cohorts who should be de-risking.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: The marginal buyer is already fully invested — a sentiment ceiling for equities and a positioning floor for bonds as a contrarian long.
insights.quote: 73% of of the household financial asset mixes in equities

insights.claim: Market vane sentiment near 78 has never been that high and portfolio manager cash ratios near 1% have never been that low — extremes not even seen in the late 1990s — and with cash that thin, a redemption cycle would force managers to sell into weakness.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Identifies the liquidity accelerant: any drawdown that triggers fund outflows becomes mechanically self-reinforcing rather than dip-bought.
insights.quote: portfolio manager cash ratios are down to almost 1%. What happens if we start getting a redemption cycle and then they're forced to sell?

insights.claim: With a CAPE around 40 and a negative equity risk premium — a 2.5% earnings yield against a 3% real long-bond yield — the market is effectively pricing equities as a riskless asset class.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A negative ERP is the cleanest quantitative case for shifting the marginal dollar from US equities to duration and non-US equity.
insights.quote: When the ERP goes negative, it's the stock market's way of telling you uh that equities are no longer as an asset class uh a a risky asset class.

insights.claim: Over half the market is now passive, with roughly 40% of the index concentrated in 10 stocks and eight of those 10 in the same AI trade, so index investors believe they are diversified while owning the most concentrated S&P 500 of all time.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Passive flows are the transmission mechanism that turns an AI-specific derating into a broad household wealth shock.
insights.quote: Diversification has become a dirty 15-letter word.

insights.claim: Rosenberg uses Jamie Dimon's October 2025 bubble call — which allowed for another 20% of upside — to argue the market is in extra innings rather than the third, sixth or ninth, and the S&P is up 16-17% in the eleven months since.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Bubble recognition is not a timing signal; the actionable posture is staying invested with lower beta and hedges rather than going flat.
insights.quote: we're not in the third inning. We're not in the sixth inning. We're not even in the ninth inning. We're we're in extra innings, which means that we are on borrow time.

themes.theme: Fed Regime Change and the Rate Backup

insights.claim: Two-thirds of the recent backup in 10-year Treasury yields occurred on just three days — June 17, July 29 and August 28 — each a day the new Fed chair spoke, making Fed rhetoric rather than fiscal supply the dominant driver.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: If the yield move is rhetoric-driven, it can reverse just as fast on a communications shift — a cleaner catalyst than waiting on deficit news.
insights.quote: twothirds of the backup and 10-year Treasury yields in the past several months have happened on three days

insights.claim: Repricing the Fed from two cuts to two hikes is worth roughly 60 basis points of the roughly 80 basis point rise in the 10-year note, because the cost of carry is the most influential determinant of yields out the curve.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Quantifies the reversal trade: a swing back to a neutral or easing bias mechanically reclaims most of the yield backup.
insights.quote: So 3/4 of the increase has actually come from the reset of Fed expectations

insights.claim: Higher oil prices and the $40 trillion debt narrative are not what pushed yields up — TIPS breakevens have not driven nominal yields, and the debt was already $39 trillion in February when the 10-year yielded below 4%.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Debunks the consensus bond-vigilante story; investors trading long-end shorts on deficit headlines are fitting narrative to price action.
insights.quote: you got a lot of people that like to fit the narrative into the price action

insights.claim: The new Fed chair's preferred gauge — real private final sales running at 3% — strips out the foreign trade sector even though much of the AI spending boom requires imported inputs, an internal contradiction that undermines confidence in his read of the economy.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A chair working from an incoherent dashboard raises policy-error risk in both directions and widens the distribution of rate outcomes.
insights.quote: how can you exclude imports part of net trade from that calculation, which is what his favorite economic indicator does?

insights.claim: The chair's hawkish talking points — that over half of PCE deflator components run above 3%, that commodity prices matter for inflation, and that wages are not a reliable inflation indicator — are analytically weak because the US is a service-sector economy where labor costs dominate and commodity pass-through is muted.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Suggests the hawkish repricing rests on statistics that will not be confirmed by incoming data, favoring the fade.
insights.quote: he's basically taking economics 101 and turning it upside down

insights.claim: Jackson Hole doubled market-implied odds of a September 17 rate hike from about 30% to about 60%, despite the Dallas Fed trimmed mean PCE running at 2.3% and recent benign CPI and PCE prints.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Sets up an asymmetric bond trade: benign inflation data against 60% hike odds means positive carry on being long duration into the meeting.

insights.claim: Rosenberg does not think the Fed will hike on September 17 because the chair needs seven votes and, even with three July dissenters, likely does not have them — and a no-hike after hawkish guidance would damage his credibility and add to market confusion.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A no-hike against 60% priced odds is the specific event that could trigger the Fed-expectations reset behind his bond call.
insights.quote: Okay, I don't think they're going to raise rates.

insights.claim: The November 4 Treasury refunding announcement is the under-discussed catalyst for bonds: Rosenberg expects a form of operation twist on the issuance side, shifting supply toward bills and the front end and away from the long end.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A dated, tradeable catalyst that almost nobody is positioned for; long-end duration bought ahead of it carries event optionality.
insights.quote: I'll tell you right now in the leadup to November the 4th, I'll probably be buying more bonds

insights.claim: The November 2023 refunding is the direct analog: the same issuance shift came right as 10-year yields peaked at 5%, and within three months the 10-year had fallen about 100 basis points.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Gives a historical magnitude for the trade and a template for what a supply-composition surprise does to the long end.

insights.claim: The average maturity of outstanding federal debt is currently 60 months versus a historical 71 months, giving the Treasury latitude to deliver a large positive supply surprise to the bond market.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Quantifies the room the issuer has to manipulate long-end supply — the Treasury, not just the Fed, is a swing factor in yields.
insights.quote: right now the average maturity on outstanding federal debt is 60 month

insights.claim: Rosenberg expects a bull steepener and sees a 50 basis point rally in the 10-year note as achievable from current levels, while stopping short of forecasting a return below 4%.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A concrete target for duration longs and a steepener expression rather than an outright long-bond bet.
insights.quote: do I think we can get a 50 basis point rally in the 10-year note from where we are today? Absolutely.

insights.claim: Rosenberg's model portfolio holds 10-year and 2-year notes but not the long bond, though a 3% real yield at the long end is described as a comfy cushion he is now considering, in an asset class that is only 7% of household holdings and widely detested.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Shows how a bond bull is actually expressing it — intermediate duration first, long end only as real yields stay above 3%.
insights.quote: a 3% real yield is a real comfy cushion. So, I'm thinking about it.

insights.claim: Rosenberg is avoiding financials and consumer discretionary and is not participating in the AI trade at all, yet runs roughly 55% equities — his bearish label comes from not owning the S&P 500 rather than from being out of stocks.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A template for staying invested with negative correlation to the dominant trade instead of going to cash.
insights.quote: I would suggest not buying the S&P stock. ever.

insights.claim: Europe is Rosenberg's favored developed market because it has fiscal tailwinds just as US fiscal support ends, better valuations and equity risk premium, and a well-diversified index with little AI exposure.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A liquid, index-level way to own equity beta that is not the AI trade, with a fiscal impulse crossing over as the US impulse fades.
insights.quote: You just buy the European index. It doesn't have a lot of AI exposure. It's very well balanced.

insights.claim: The Citigroup economic surprise index for Europe is at roughly a four-year high while the US measure is bordering on a six-month low, supporting the relative-growth case for European over US assets.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A trackable relative-momentum indicator to time or size the Europe-over-US rotation.

insights.claim: Rosenberg is long emerging market equities but deliberately underweight Taiwan and Korea because they are part and parcel of the AI trade, preferring Japan, India and Brazil instead.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Buying a standard EM index reimports the AI correlation he is trying to avoid — country selection is the whole point of the trade.
insights.quote: we're being very mindful about not having too much exposure to Taiwan and Korea because they're part and parcel of this whole AI trade

insights.claim: Commodities and basic materials are Rosenberg's buy-and-hold rather than a trade — oil, pipelines, energy infrastructure, rare earths and base metals — because future supply-demand curves point to a broad basic-materials deficit for years.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Multi-year structural exposure that behaves differently from the AI complex and can be held through a de-rating of US equities.
insights.quote: This is not a trade. This is not a trade.

insights.claim: Rosenberg is simultaneously a disinflationist on services and a bull on commodities, arguing services inflation matters far more for the CPI and PCE deflator than commodity prices do.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Resolves the apparent contradiction of owning commodities while expecting rate cuts — commodity inflation does not block Fed easing.
insights.quote: So, I'm a disinflationist in services, but I'm a bull on commodities.

insights.claim: Rosenberg owns a lot of healthcare but deliberately does not own consumer staples, because staples will be hit by globally rising food prices even though both sectors are uncorrelated with the AI trade.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A nuance most defensive rotations miss: input-cost inflation makes staples a worse AI hedge than healthcare.
insights.quote: we don't have consumer staples cuz we think that they will be hit by the fact that food prices are going up globally

insights.claim: Rosenberg's model portfolio runs a 0.4 beta to the S&P 500, 0.7 to a 60/40 and a 1.1 Sharpe ratio, and is up 60% over three and a half years without owning a single AI stock or Bitcoin — earlier winners being Asia, aerospace and defense, gold, silver and the miners, and healthcare.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Evidence that a low-beta, non-AI, thematic book has kept pace without the concentration risk — the core marketing and analytical case for his approach.
insights.quote: I've had this portfolio for three and a half years and it's up 60%. I haven't owned one AI stock and it's a low to medium risk portfolio.

insights.claim: Rosenberg's research is being turned into a publicly traded ETF under the ticker ROSY, managed by Toronto-based Corton Capital, listing September 9 initially on the TSX with both Canadian dollar and US dollar versions.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A new listed vehicle that makes his low-beta, non-AI allocation directly investable and its holdings publicly trackable.
insights.quote: It's going to be listed on September the 9th. The ticker is going to be ROSY and it will be listed uh initially on the TSX.

themes.theme: New Harbor Hedging and Tape Read

insights.claim: New Harbor just bought S&P 500 put options struck at 7200 with the index near 7,700, expiring mid-October, which would effectively take about 20% of equity exposure off the table if triggered.
insights.speaker: John Lodra
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable hedge structure and strike level marking where professionals see the first meaningful downside break.
insights.quote: If the S&P dropped be drops below 7200, those put options will kick in and take effectively about 20% equity exposure off the table.

insights.claim: With the VIX around 15, that S&P put hedge cost only about 12 basis points at the total portfolio level, making downside insurance close to negligible in cost at current implied volatility.
insights.speaker: John Lodra
insights.so_what: Cheap convexity is available now; the cost of waiting until volatility rises is the real risk for unhedged portfolios.
insights.quote: it was about 12 basis points of cost at the portfolio level

insights.claim: New Harbor runs about 50% equities and about 32% fixed income at roughly a 5-year average duration — shorter than the aggregate bond index — including a 7-12% long-Treasury position and some non-dollar foreign bonds, while explicitly not being bond bulls.
insights.speaker: John Lodra
insights.so_what: Shows an advisor barbelling short duration with a modest long-Treasury sleeve rather than making Rosenberg's full duration bet.

insights.claim: New Harbor's technical breadth indicators had strengthened notably across market caps and into lagging sectors like financials and healthcare, but have since weakened enough to justify hedging without cutting equity exposure.
insights.speaker: John Lodra
insights.so_what: Illustrates a defined escalation ladder — hedge first on breadth deterioration, reduce exposure only if price levels break.
insights.quote: Nothing that screams like fire alarm, but enough that we felt that it was prudent

insights.claim: Mike Preston places the market between greed and delusion on the sentiment cycle and expects a blowoff top above 8,500 on the S&P 500 in a short period, warning that the final two stages could last only about a month rather than years.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston
insights.so_what: A specific upside target and a short expected duration for it — argues for staying long with hedges rather than shorting the top.
insights.quote: I think that we're still going to get a blowoff top somewhere above 8,500 in a short period of time on the S&P

insights.claim: S&P 500 profit margins have run at 11-12% for over a decade against a long-term norm near 8%, sustained largely by government deficit spending, so a CAPE of 40 is being calculated on peak margins that could revert to 8% or even 6%.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston
insights.so_what: Stacks margin-reversion risk on top of multiple-compression risk — the two together imply a far deeper earnings drawdown than headline valuation suggests.
insights.quote: we've been trending around or sitting around 11 or 12% for the last decade plus because of all of this deficit spending by the government

insights.claim: Silver's correction from its late-January high has now completed three legs down — usually the maximum in a counter-trend move — and broke out of its downtrend in early August, with SLV around 60 (roughly 66 spot) and the next resistance near 67 on SLV, about 73 spot.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston
insights.so_what: Gives explicit levels for re-entering silver after the drawdown and a defined resistance target to trade against.

insights.claim: The Jackson Hole hawkish surprise that doubled hike odds knocked spot silver from about 64 to 57 in three days, but the bounce off the 50-day moving average suggests that pullback is complete.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston
insights.so_what: Confirms precious metals are trading on Fed-expectation repricing, so a Fed-expectations reset would be a direct upside catalyst for metals as well as bonds.

insights.claim: Gold and silver miners are tracing cup-and-handle bases across the group — Eldorado Gold, Wheaton Precious Metals, Franco-Nevada, and Newmont, the only miner in the S&P 500, which made a new high before forming its handle.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston
insights.so_what: A group-wide pattern rather than single-name setups implies a sector breakout signal rather than idiosyncratic moves.

insights.claim: A break above roughly 106 on GDX would complete the cup-and-handle breakout and is the trigger point Preston is watching, with target prices potentially near double recent highs on the miners.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston
insights.so_what: One number to watch as the actionable confirmation signal for adding precious-metals equity exposure.
insights.quote: watch for a breakthrough of 106 or so on GDX and uh that would mean the cup and handle um breakout would be complete
